about: A closer look at one page of Tau HUD a day, in this order, each once. The alerts service (infra/alerts/alerts.py, maybe_deepdive) reads this file from the site every 10 minutes and posts the next one not yet posted at 13:00 UTC on Telegram; every second one also goes to X. Add new pages at the end; an id is posted once, ever. Texts are plain (no HTML; the bot escapes them); x = the lines of the X post, trimmed to 280 by the bot, which adds the footer and #TauNet $AGRS. Nothing here is affiliated with IDNI; test AGRS have no value.

posts.title: Start here: Tau in four steps
posts.text:
Most people's first question is what you can actually do on the Tau testnet. The Start page answers it in four steps, each in your browser, nothing to install: make a test wallet, give your account a rule the chain itself checks, watch a block seal it, and feed Agorzilla with it.
Every step ends with the real transaction on the explorer, so you see what you did instead of reading that you did it. Test AGRS have no value; the point is the rule, not the money.
posts.try: ten minutes, phone or laptop. The wallet is made for you on the first page.
x: 🔎 A closer look: Start here, Tau in four steps
Make a test wallet, give your account a rule the chain itself checks, watch a block seal it, feed Agorzilla. All in the browser, nothing to install, test AGRS have no value.

posts.title: White Rabbit Key: an island election on the testnet
posts.text:
Four candidates, five days, laws, pacts, embassy envelopes and rumours on Radio Coco, and a Book in the lighthouse that nobody can edit. White Rabbit Key is a small hand-painted election game, and the twist is that every move you make is one real transaction on Tau Testnet Alpha: a speech, a law, a pact.
Since the island became one shared place, everyone plays their own campaign and the island adds up what everyone did that day. The Key Crier reports it here every morning.

x: 🔎 A closer look: White Rabbit Key
An island election game where every move is a real transaction on Tau Testnet Alpha: speeches, laws, pacts, rumours on Radio Coco, and a Book nobody can edit. Four candidates, five days.

posts.title: The testnet wallet: an account with its own rules
posts.text:
A Tau wallet is not a key and a balance; it is an account with rules. The Tau HUD wallet runs in your browser and shows what that means: send, send with a way back, ask a friend to co-sign, vote on the chain's rules, and agree on shared rules with others in a Pakt.
It is non-custodial and testnet only. The rules are written in the Tau language and checked by the chain, not by the wallet: a transaction the rule refuses never gets into a block.
posts.try: give your account one rule and then try to break it.
x: 🔎 A closer look: the testnet wallet

On Tau a wallet is an account with rules: send with a way back, co-sign with a friend, vote on the chain's rules, agree shared rules in a Pakt. The chain checks the rules, not the wallet. Testnet only.

posts.title: The rules wall: every personal rule on the testnet
posts.text:
Every rule that an account gave itself on Tau Testnet Alpha, read straight from the blocks. The rules wall is the best place to see what people actually write when a chain lets them: spending limits, waiting times, rules that need a second signature.
If you agree with one, you can take it for your own account with one click. That is a real transaction, and the wall counts how many accounts adopted each rule.

x: 🔎 A closer look: the rules wall
Every personal rule that accounts gave themselves on Tau Testnet Alpha, read from the blocks. Agree with one? Take it for your own account: a real transaction, counted on the wall.

posts.title: The explorer: what happened to a transaction
posts.text:
A block explorer usually tells you that a transaction is in a block. The Tau HUD explorer tells you what happened on the way: its path from the queue to the block, which rules checked it, and whether a transaction that looks like it is waiting is really waiting or already sealed.
That last part matters on this testnet: sealed transactions can still be listed as pending by the node, a finding we reported to IDNI. The explorer tells the two apart.

x: 🔎 A closer look: the explorer
Not only that a transaction is in a block, but what happened on the way: its path from the queue to the block, which rules checked it, and whether a waiting transaction is really waiting.

posts.title: The account view: a balance and the rules around it
posts.text:
Look up any account on Tau Testnet Alpha and you get more than a balance over time: the rules it set for its own money, the rules others offered it, and what it refused.
It is the page that shows the difference between Tau and a plain ledger. Two accounts with the same balance can have very different lives, because one of them promised something and the chain holds it to that.

x: 🔎 A closer look: the account view

posts.title: The proposal tracker: how the chain changes its own rules
posts.text:
On Tau the rules of the chain are changed by the chain's users, not by a hard fork: a rule change is proposed, the validators agree, and at a set block it is in force. The proposal tracker lists every one on Tau Testnet Alpha: proposed, agreed, in force or dropped, with what each would change in plain words.
This channel is its feed: every real rule change is posted here when it is proposed, agreed and in force.

Every rule change on Tau Testnet Alpha: proposed, agreed, in force or dropped, each with what it changes in plain words. The chain's rules change by agreement, never by decree.

posts.title: Vote on Tau: a ready command for every open proposal
posts.text:
You can vote on Tau Testnet Alpha's rules yourself, with your own node and your own key. The Vote page gives you a ready vote command for every open proposal and a ready proposal of your own, and lets you practise every step on the simulation first.
At the moment the network admits votes from validators only; the page says so and shows what would count. The practice votes you see in Testnet today come from here.

How to vote on Tau Testnet Alpha's rules yourself: your own node, your key, a ready vote command for every open proposal. Practise every step on the simulation first.

posts.title: The rule playground: write a rule, let the chain check it
posts.text:
Write your own Tau rule and put it through the same checks the Tau Testnet Alpha applies, before it costs you a transaction. The playground shows what the checker says in plain words, line by line.
Then take a simulated validator seat and vote a rule change in: the simulation runs the real consensus steps at a pace you can watch, and other visitors can vote on your proposal too.

posts.title: Missions: six short exercises on a practice chain
posts.text:
Six missions on a practice chain in your browser: vote a rule in, get one refused, let one fail at two thirds, lower the bar, survive a validator outage, switch to proof of stake. Each takes a few minutes and ends where to see the same thing on the real Tau testnet.
It is the quickest way to understand why a rule change on Tau is not a vote but an agreement, and what happens when the agreement is not there.

posts.title: What if: move the chain's dials and watch
posts.text:
Move the block time, the number of validators and the votes a rule change needs, and watch a simulated chain react: short splits, missed blocks, slow or stuck agreement.
It is a toy, but an honest one: the same thresholds the testnet uses, so you see why a bar of two thirds behaves differently from a majority, and why one validator going quiet can stop everything.

posts.title: Chain time travel: every block, every rule in force
posts.text:
Scrub through every block of Tau Testnet Alpha and see which rules were in force at that moment, who voted, and when each agreed change took effect.
It turns the proposal tracker into a timeline: you can stand on any block and read the chain's rulebook as it was then, which is the thing a chain that changes its own rules needs most.

posts.title: Testnet stats: how the chain is doing
posts.text:
Block times, transactions, active accounts, dropped transactions and chain restarts, read from our own node and not from anyone's press release.
The restarts and drops are the interesting part. A testnet is where things break, and this page keeps the record of when they did, which is also where our findings and the road to mainnet start.

posts.title: Status: one health score for the testnet
posts.text:
Is the Tau testnet healthy right now? One score from 0 to 100, built from the node's sync, the pace of blocks, peers, restarts and the relay that serves this site, with the last 30 days underneath.
When the score falls, this channel says so; when it is back, the channel says that too. The page shows the why behind the number.

posts.title: Findings: the bugs we found while running a node
posts.text:
Running a node for tauhud.com turns up things: sealed transactions still listed as pending, a node that stays behind the network, a peer list that forgets its bootnode. The findings page lists each one with how to reproduce it, its status at IDNI, and how to report your own.
The bot in this channel watches for the same patterns live and posts when one starts and when it is over.

The bugs we found in Tau Testnet Alpha while running a node for tauhud.com, how to reproduce each, their status at IDNI, and how to report your own.

posts.title: Road to mainnet: what we think should be fixed first
posts.text:
What we found on Tau Testnet Alpha that we think should be fixed before mainnet, each item with its proof and a path to a fix. It is our view from running a node, not IDNI's plan, and it says so.
You can comment on any item. Disagreement is welcome; a testnet is for finding out.

posts.title: Community nodes: run one, get a badge
posts.text:
People who run a Tau testnet node with the Tau HUD kit: how long each has been running, how steadily, and whether it agrees with our chain. A node that sees a different chain is the first sign of a split, and this page would show it.
The kit is one command; the badge is for your README or forum signature and updates itself.

posts.title: Developers: the live testnet on your own site

The API is the same one Tau HUD's own pages use, served from our relay; the docs page has a working example for each call.

posts.title: The Daily Consensus: a 1920s newspaper about Tau
posts.text:
A newspaper in the style of the 1920s about Tau and Testnet Alpha: twelve years of the project, the chain that changes its own rules, letters, obituaries, puzzles. Turn the pages with a click or a tap.
A new edition comes out every Monday morning and is announced here with the week's numbers. The puzzles have answers on the last page; the obituaries are for rules that were voted out.
